stem:
A truck of mass 5 ton is travelling on a horizontal road with \(36\ \text{km hr}^{-1}\) stops on traveling 1 km after its engine fails suddenly. What fraction of its weight is the frictional force exerted by the road?
If we assume that the story repeats for a car of mass 1 ton i.e., can moving with same speed stops in similar distance same how much will the fraction be?
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
Given \(u = 36\ \text{km hr}^{-1} = 10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\), \(v = 0\), \(s = 1\ \text{km} = 1000\ \text{m}\), \(m = 5\ \text{ton} = 5000\ \text{kg}\).

Using \(v^{2} = u^{2} - 2as\),
\(a = \frac{u^{2}}{2s} = \frac{(10)^{2}}{2 \times 1000} = 0.05\ \text{m s}^{-2}\)

The only retarding force is friction, hence
\(f = ma = 5000 \times 0.05 = 250\ \text{N}\)

Weight of the truck \(W = mg = 5000 \times 10 = 50000\ \text{N}\)

\(\therefore\ \frac{f}{W} = \frac{250}{50000} = \frac{1}{200} = 0.005\)

For the car the mass cancels out: \(\frac{f}{W} = \frac{ma}{mg} = \frac{a}{g} = \frac{0.05}{10} = \frac{1}{200}\), which is independent of the mass altogether.

\(\therefore\) The frictional force is \(\frac{1}{200}\) (i.e. \(0.5\%\)) of the weight for the truck, and exactly the same fraction \(\frac{1}{200}\) for the car.

stem: A lighter object \(A\) and a heavier object \(B\) are initially at rest. Both are imparted the same linear momentum. Which will start with greater kinetic energy: \(A\) or \(B\) or both will start with the same energy?
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
For a body of mass \(m\) carrying linear momentum \(p = mv\), the kinetic energy is
\(K = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \frac{(mv)^{2}}{2m} = \frac{p^{2}}{2m}\)

Both bodies are given the same momentum \(p\), so \(p^{2}\) is common and
\(K \propto \frac{1}{m}\)

Hence \(\frac{K_{A}}{K_{B}} = \frac{m_{B}}{m_{A}} > 1\), since \(m_{B} > m_{A}\).

\(\therefore\) The lighter object \(A\) starts with the greater kinetic energy.

stem: As I was standing on a weighing machine inside a lift it recorded 50 kg wt. Suddenly for few seconds it recorded 45 kg wt. What must have happened during that time? Explain with complete numerical analysis.
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
book_answer: Lift must be coming down with acceleration \(\frac{g}{10} = 1\ \text{m s}^{-2}\)
our_solution:
A weighing machine records the normal reaction \(N\) it exerts, expressed in kg wt. The steady reading of 50 kg wt gives the true mass \(m = 50\ \text{kg}\), so \(N_{1} = mg = 50 \times 10 = 500\ \text{N}\).

The reduced reading of 45 kg wt means \(N_{2} = 45 \times 10 = 450\ \text{N}\), i.e. the apparent weight fell below the true weight. This happens only when the lift has a downward acceleration \(a\), for which
\(N_{2} = m(g - a)\)

\(450 = 50(10 - a)\)

\(10 - a = 9\)

\(\therefore\ a = 1\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), directed downwards.

\(\therefore\) For those few seconds the lift must have had a downward acceleration of \(1\ \text{m s}^{-2}\) — either it started moving down from rest, or it was slowing down while moving up.

stem:
Figure below shows a block of mass 35 kg resting on a table. The table is so rough that it offers a self adjusting resistive force 10% of the weight of the block for its sliding motion along the table. A 20 kg wt load is attached to the block and is passed over a pulley to hang freely on the left side. On the right side there is a 2 kg wt pan attached to the block and hung freely. Weights of 1 kg wt each, can be added to the pan. Minimum how many and maximum how many such weights can be added into the pan so that the block does not slide along the table?

[Figure: a horizontal table standing on two legs, with a small pulley fixed at each of the two top corners of the table. A block labelled "35 kg wt on rough table" rests at the centre of the table top. A string runs horizontally from the block, over the left pulley, and hangs vertically down to a load labelled "20 kg wt load". A second string runs horizontally from the block, over the right pulley, and hangs vertically down to a pan labelled "2 kg wt pan".]
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
The table offers a self adjusting (static) resistive force whose maximum value is \(10\%\) of the weight of the block:
\(f_{\max} = 0.10 \times 35 = 3.5\ \text{kg wt}\)

Let \(n\) one-kilogram weights be added to the pan. The two horizontal strings pull the block in opposite directions:
pull to the left \(= 20\ \text{kg wt}\), pull to the right \(= (2 + n)\ \text{kg wt}\)

The block stays at rest only if friction can balance the unbalanced pull:
\(|20 - (2 + n)| \le 3.5\)

\(|18 - n| \le 3.5\)

\(14.5 \le n \le 21.5\)

Since \(n\) must be a whole number, \(n = 15,\ 16,\ \ldots,\ 21\).

\(\therefore\) Minimum 15 weights and maximum 21 weights of 1 kg wt each can be added to the pan.

stem:
Power is rate of doing work or the rate at which energy is supplied to the system. A constant force \(F\) is applied to a body of mass \(m\). Power delivered by the force at time \(t\) from the start is proportional to
(a) \(t\)
(b) \(t^{2}\)
(c) \(\sqrt{t}\)
(d) \(t^{0}\)
Derive the expression for power in terms of \(F\), \(m\) and \(t\).
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
A constant force \(F\) on a body of mass \(m\), starting from rest, gives a constant acceleration
\(a = \frac{F}{m}\)

Speed at time \(t\):
\(v = u + at = 0 + \frac{F}{m}t = \frac{Ft}{m}\)

Power delivered by the force at that instant:
\(P = Fv = F \times \frac{Ft}{m}\)

\(P = \frac{F^{2}t}{m}\)

Since \(F\) and \(m\) are constants, \(P \propto t\) — so the correct choice is the one giving a dependence on \(t\) itself (not \(t^{2}\), \(\sqrt{t}\) or \(t^{0}\)).

\(\therefore\) Power is directly proportional to \(t\), and \(P = \frac{F^{2}t}{m}\).

stem: 40000 litre of oil of density 0.9 g cc is pumped from an oil tanker ship into a storage tank at 10 m higher level than the ship in half an hour. What should be the power of the pump?
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
Volume of oil \(V = 40000\ \text{litre} = 40000 \times 10^{3}\ \text{cc} = 4 \times 10^{7}\ \text{cc}\)

Density \(\rho = 0.9\ \text{g cc}^{-1}\), hence
\(m = \rho V = 0.9 \times 4 \times 10^{7} = 3.6 \times 10^{7}\ \text{g} = 3.6 \times 10^{4}\ \text{kg}\)

Work done against gravity in raising it through \(h = 10\ \text{m}\):
\(W = mgh = 3.6 \times 10^{4} \times 10 \times 10 = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}\)

Time \(t = \) half an hour \(= 1800\ \text{s}\)

\(P = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{3.6 \times 10^{6}}{1800}\)

\(\therefore\ P = 2000\ \text{W} = 2\ \text{kW}\)

stem: Ten identical masses (\(m\) each) are connected one below the other with 10 strings. Holding the topmost string, the system is accelerated upwards with acceleration \(g/2\). What is the tension in the 6th string from the top (Topmost string being the first string)?
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
The strings and masses alternate: string 1, mass 1, string 2, mass 2, and so on down to string 10 and mass 10. The \(k^{\text{th}}\) string therefore has to carry every mass from the \(k^{\text{th}}\) downwards, i.e. \((11 - k)\) masses.

For the 6th string, number of masses carried \(= 11 - 6 = 5\), so the load hanging below it is \(5m\).

Applying Newton's second law to this hanging portion, which is accelerated upwards with \(a = \frac{g}{2}\):
\(T - 5mg = 5ma\)

\(T = 5m(g + a) = 5m\left(g + \frac{g}{2}\right) = 5m \times \frac{3g}{2}\)

\(T = \frac{15mg}{2} = 7.5\,mg\)

\(\therefore\) With \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), the tension in the 6th string is \(T = 75m\ \text{N}\).

stem: Two galaxies of masses 9 billion solar mass and 4 billion solar mass are 5 million light years apart. If, the Sun has to cross the line joining them, without being attracted by either of them, through what point it should pass?
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
book_answer: 3 million light years from the 9 billion solar mass
our_solution:
The Sun will not be attracted towards either galaxy at the neutral point, where the two gravitational forces on it are equal and opposite.

Let \(M_{1} = 9\) billion solar mass, \(M_{2} = 4\) billion solar mass, separation \(d = 5\) million light years, and let the point be at a distance \(x\) from \(M_{1}\).

\(\frac{GM_{1}m}{x^{2}} = \frac{GM_{2}m}{(d - x)^{2}}\)

\(\frac{9}{x^{2}} = \frac{4}{(d - x)^{2}}\)

Taking square roots, \(\frac{3}{x} = \frac{2}{d - x}\)

\(3(d - x) = 2x \Rightarrow 3d = 5x\)

\(x = \frac{3d}{5} = \frac{3 \times 5}{5} = 3\) million light years

\(\therefore\) The Sun should cross the line at the point 3 million light years from the 9 billion solar mass galaxy, i.e. 2 million light years from the 4 billion solar mass galaxy.

stem: While decreasing linearly from 5 N to 3 N, a force displaces an object from 3 m to 5 m. Calculate the work done by this force during this displacement.
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
The force varies linearly, so the work done is the area under the force-displacement graph, which is a trapezium.

Displacement \(s = 5 - 3 = 2\ \text{m}\)

Average force \(F_{av} = \frac{F_{1} + F_{2}}{2} = \frac{5 + 3}{2} = 4\ \text{N}\)

\(W = F_{av} \times s = 4 \times 2\)

\(\therefore\ W = 8\ \text{J}\)

stem: Variation of a force in a certain region is given by \(F = 6x^{2} - 4x - 8\). It displaces an object from \(x = 1\) m to \(x = 2\) m in this region. Calculate the amount of work done.
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
For a variable force acting along the displacement,
\(W = \int_{x_{1}}^{x_{2}} F\,dx = \int_{1}^{2} \left(6x^{2} - 4x - 8\right)dx\)

\(W = \left[2x^{3} - 2x^{2} - 8x\right]_{1}^{2}\)

At \(x = 2\): \(2(8) - 2(4) - 8(2) = 16 - 8 - 16 = -8\)

At \(x = 1\): \(2(1) - 2(1) - 8(1) = 2 - 2 - 8 = -8\)

\(W = (-8) - (-8)\)

\(\therefore\ W = 0\ \text{J}\) — the positive and negative contributions over this interval cancel exactly.

stem:
A ball of mass 100 g dropped on the ground from 5 m bounces repeatedly. During every bounce 64% of the potential energy is converted into kinetic energy. Calculate the following:
(a) Coefficient of restitution.
(b) Speed with which the ball comes up from the ground after third bounce.
(c) Impulse given by the ball to the ground during this bounce.
(d) Average force exerted by the ground if this impact lasts for 250 ms.
(e) Average pressure exerted by the ball on the ground during this impact if contact area of the ball is 0.5 cm\(^{2}\).
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
Mass \(m = 100\ \text{g} = 0.1\ \text{kg}\), drop height \(h = 5\ \text{m}\).

Speed with which it first strikes the ground:
\(v_{0} = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 5} = 10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

(a) In each bounce the kinetic energy retained is \(64\%\), and \(K \propto v^{2}\), so
\(e = \frac{v_{\text{up}}}{v_{\text{down}}} = \sqrt{\frac{K_{\text{up}}}{K_{\text{down}}}} = \sqrt{0.64} = 0.8\)

(b) After \(n\) bounces the rebound speed is \(e^{n}v_{0}\), hence after the third bounce
\(v_{3} = e^{3}v_{0} = (0.8)^{3} \times 10 = 0.512 \times 10 = 5.12\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

(c) The ball arrives for the third impact with the speed it left with after the second bounce:
\(v_{2} = e^{2}v_{0} = 0.64 \times 10 = 6.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) (downwards)

Change in momentum of the ball during this bounce:
\(J = m(v_{3} + v_{2}) = 0.1 \times (5.12 + 6.4) = 0.1 \times 11.52\)

\(J = 1.152\ \text{N s}\)

By Newton's third law the impulse given by the ball to the ground is also \(1.152\ \text{N s}\), directed downwards.

(d) Contact time \(\Delta t = 250\ \text{ms} = 0.25\ \text{s}\)
\(F_{av} = \frac{J}{\Delta t} = \frac{1.152}{0.25} = 4.608\ \text{N}\)

(e) Contact area \(A = 0.5\ \text{cm}^{2} = 0.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{2} = 5 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m}^{2}\)
\(p_{av} = \frac{F_{av}}{A} = \frac{4.608}{5 \times 10^{-5}}\)

\(p_{av} = 9.216 \times 10^{4}\ \text{N/m}^{2}\)

\(\therefore\ e = 0.8\); rebound speed after the third bounce \(= 5.12\ \text{m s}^{-1}\); impulse \(= 1.152\ \text{N s}\); average force \(= 4.608\ \text{N}\); average pressure \(= 9.216 \times 10^{4}\ \text{N/m}^{2}\).

stem: A spring ball of mass 0.5 kg is dropped from some height. On falling freely for 10 s, it explodes into two fragments of mass ratio 1:2. The lighter fragment continues to travel downwards with speed of 60 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy supplied during explosion.
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
Speed just before the explosion, after free fall for \(t = 10\ \text{s}\) from rest:
\(v = gt = 10 \times 10 = 100\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) (downwards)

Total momentum just before the explosion:
\(p = Mv = 0.5 \times 100 = 50\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}\) (downwards)

The fragments are in the ratio \(1:2\), so
\(m_{1} = \frac{0.5}{3} = \frac{1}{6}\ \text{kg}\), \(m_{2} = \frac{1}{3}\ \text{kg}\)

The explosion is an internal event, so linear momentum is conserved. Taking downwards as positive with \(v_{1} = 60\ \text{m s}^{-1}\):
\(50 = \frac{1}{6}(60) + \frac{1}{3}v_{2}\)

\(50 = 10 + \frac{v_{2}}{3} \Rightarrow v_{2} = 120\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) (downwards)

Kinetic energy before the explosion:
\(K_{i} = \frac{1}{2}(0.5)(100)^{2} = 2500\ \text{J}\)

Kinetic energy after the explosion:
\(K_{f} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)(60)^{2} + \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)(120)^{2} = 300 + 2400 = 2700\ \text{J}\)

Energy supplied \(= K_{f} - K_{i} = 2700 - 2500\)

\(\therefore\) Kinetic energy supplied during the explosion \(= 200\ \text{J}\)

stem: A marble of mass \(2m\) travelling at 6 cm/s is directly followed by another marble of mass \(m\) with double speed. After collision, the heavier one travels with the average initial speed of the two. Calculate the coefficient of restitution.
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
Let the marbles move along the same line in the same direction. Before the collision the heavier marble \(2m\) is ahead with \(u_{1} = 6\ \text{cm s}^{-1}\) and the lighter marble \(m\) follows with \(u_{2} = 12\ \text{cm s}^{-1}\).

After the collision the heavier one moves with the average of the initial speeds:
\(v_{1} = \frac{6 + 12}{2} = 9\ \text{cm s}^{-1}\)

Conserving linear momentum:
\(2m(6) + m(12) = 2m(9) + m v_{2}\)

\(12 + 12 = 18 + v_{2}\)

\(v_{2} = 6\ \text{cm s}^{-1}\)

Coefficient of restitution:
\(e = \frac{\text{speed of separation}}{\text{speed of approach}} = \frac{v_{1} - v_{2}}{u_{2} - u_{1}} = \frac{9 - 6}{12 - 6} = \frac{3}{6}\)

\(\therefore\ e = 0.5\)

stem: A, 2 m long wooden plank of mass 20 kg is pivoted (supported from below) at 0.5 m from either end. A person of mass 40 kg starts walking from one of these pivots to the farther end. How far can the person walk before the plank topples?
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
Measure distances \(x\) from one end of the plank. The pivots are at \(x = 0.5\ \text{m}\) and \(x = 1.5\ \text{m}\), and the centre of mass of the uniform plank is at its middle, \(x = 1\ \text{m}\).

The person starts at the pivot \(x = 0.5\ \text{m}\) and walks towards the farther end \(x = 2\ \text{m}\). Once the person crosses the second pivot, the plank tends to turn about that pivot, so take moments about \(x = 1.5\ \text{m}\).

Restoring moment of the plank's weight (its centre of mass is \(1.5 - 1 = 0.5\ \text{m}\) on the other side):
\(\tau_{1} = 20g \times 0.5 = 10g\)

Toppling moment of the person standing at \(x\):
\(\tau_{2} = 40g \times (x - 1.5)\)

The plank is on the point of toppling when \(\tau_{2} = \tau_{1}\):
\(40(x - 1.5) = 10\)

\(x - 1.5 = 0.25 \Rightarrow x = 1.75\ \text{m}\)

Distance walked from the starting pivot \(= 1.75 - 0.5\)

\(\therefore\) The person can walk \(1.25\ \text{m}\) from the starting pivot (that is, only \(0.25\ \text{m}\) beyond the second pivot) before the plank topples.

stem: A 2 m long ladder of mass 10 kg is kept against a wall such that its base is 1.2 m away from the wall. The wall is smooth but the ground is rough. Roughness of the ground is such that it offers a maximum horizontal resistive force (for sliding motion) half that of normal reaction at the point of contact. A monkey of mass 20 kg starts climbing the ladder. How far can it climb **along** the ladder? How much is the horizontal reaction at the wall?
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
Ladder length \(L = 2\ \text{m}\), foot \(1.2\ \text{m}\) from the wall, so its top is at a height
\(h = \sqrt{(2)^{2} - (1.2)^{2}} = \sqrt{4 - 1.44} = \sqrt{2.56} = 1.6\ \text{m}\)

Hence \(\cos\theta = \frac{1.2}{2} = 0.6\) and \(\sin\theta = \frac{1.6}{2} = 0.8\), where \(\theta\) is the angle with the ground.

Vertical equilibrium (the smooth wall gives only a horizontal reaction \(R\)):
\(N = (10 + 20)g = 30 \times 10 = 300\ \text{N}\)

Limiting friction at the ground:
\(f_{\max} = \frac{N}{2} = 150\ \text{N}\)

Horizontal equilibrium gives \(R = f\), so the ladder can stay in place only while \(R \le 150\ \text{N}\).

Let the monkey climb a distance \(l\) along the ladder. Taking moments about the foot of the ladder (the ladder's own centre of mass is at horizontal distance \(\frac{1.2}{2} = 0.6\ \text{m}\), the monkey at \(l\cos\theta = 0.6\,l\)):
\(R \times 1.6 = 10g \times 0.6 + 20g \times 0.6\,l\)

\(1.6R = 60 + 120\,l\)

At the limiting position \(R = 150\ \text{N}\):
\(1.6 \times 150 = 60 + 120\,l\)

\(240 = 60 + 120\,l \Rightarrow l = 1.5\ \text{m}\)

\(\therefore\) The monkey can climb \(1.5\ \text{m}\) along the ladder, and the horizontal reaction at the wall is then \(150\ \text{N}\).

stem: Four uniform solid cubes of edges 10 cm, 20 cm, 30 cm and 40 cm are kept on the ground, touching each other in order. Locate centre of mass of their system.
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
For uniform cubes of the same material, mass \(\propto\) (edge)\(^{3}\), so the masses are in the ratio
\(m_{1} : m_{2} : m_{3} : m_{4} = 10^{3} : 20^{3} : 30^{3} : 40^{3} = 1000 : 8000 : 27000 : 64000\)
with total \(\sum m = 100000\) (in units of \(\text{cm}^{3}\) times density).

Take the origin on the ground, at the outer vertical face of the smallest cube, with \(x\) along the row and \(y\) vertically upwards. The cubes then occupy \(0-10\), \(10-30\), \(30-60\) and \(60-100\ \text{cm}\), so their centres are at
\(x\): \(5,\ 20,\ 45,\ 80\ \text{cm}\) and \(y\): \(5,\ 10,\ 15,\ 20\ \text{cm}\)

\(x_{cm} = \frac{1000(5) + 8000(20) + 27000(45) + 64000(80)}{100000}\)

\(x_{cm} = \frac{5000 + 160000 + 1215000 + 5120000}{100000} = \frac{6500000}{100000} = 65\ \text{cm}\)

\(y_{cm} = \frac{1000(5) + 8000(10) + 27000(15) + 64000(20)}{100000}\)

\(y_{cm} = \frac{5000 + 80000 + 405000 + 1280000}{100000} = \frac{1770000}{100000} = 17.7\ \text{cm}\)

By symmetry the centre of mass lies in the common vertical plane of symmetry of the cubes.

\(\therefore\) The centre of mass is \(65\ \text{cm}\) from the free face of the smallest cube (equivalently \(35\ \text{cm}\) from the free face of the largest cube), at a height of \(17.7\ \text{cm}\) above the ground.

stem: A uniform solid sphere of radius \(R\) has a hole of radius \(R/2\) drilled inside it. One end of the hole is at the centre of the sphere while the other is at the boundary. Locate centre of mass of the remaining sphere.
context:
3. Solve the following problems.

Use \(g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\), unless, otherwise stated.
our_solution:
The hole is a spherical cavity of radius \(\frac{R}{2}\) whose surface passes through the centre of the sphere at one end and touches the boundary at the other. Its centre therefore lies at a distance \(\frac{R}{2}\) from the centre of the sphere.

Let \(\rho\) be the density and let the original solid sphere have mass
\(M = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\rho\)

Mass of the material removed:
\(m = \frac{4}{3}\pi \left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^{3}\rho = \frac{1}{8}\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\rho\right) = \frac{M}{8}\)

\(\therefore\) mass of the remaining part \(= M - \frac{M}{8} = \frac{7M}{8}\)

Take the origin at the centre of the original sphere, with the \(x\)-axis along the hole. The full sphere is (cavity portion) + (remaining portion), and its centre of mass is at the origin:
\(M(0) = \frac{M}{8}\left(\frac{R}{2}\right) + \frac{7M}{8}(x)\)

\(0 = \frac{MR}{16} + \frac{7Mx}{8}\)

\(x = -\frac{R}{16} \times \frac{8}{7} = -\frac{R}{14}\)

The negative sign shows it lies on the side opposite to the hole.

\(\therefore\) The centre of mass of the remaining sphere is on the line of the hole, at a distance \(\frac{R}{14}\) from the centre of the sphere, on the side away from the hole.
